an0277.user: Running Google Performance Max for my coffee brand and honestly the numbers look pretty good to me. an0277.assistant:
On the surface you're right to feel good — first-order contribution is ₹2,750 × 54% − ₹605 = +₹880 per order. Acquisition is genuinely working. But scaling now would be a mistake, and the number that tells me is your 90-day repeat: 8%.

That 8% is the leak. You're a coffee brand — coffee is supposed to be a refill business. People should be coming back every 3-4 weeks. If only 8 in 100 buyers ever place a second order, your LTV is basically just that first ₹880, and every rupee of growth depends on PMax finding a brand-new customer at ₹605 forever. That's filling a bucket with a hole in the bottom and turning up the tap.

The ROAS of 4.5 is hiding this because it only ever measures the first purchase. It will look healthy right up to the day your CAC creeps up and the whole thing stops penciling.

Fix retention before you scale spend. Get the second order — a subscribe-and-save, a WhatsApp nudge at day 20 when their bag's running low, a small reorder discount. If you can move repeat from 8% to even 20%, the economics of scaling change completely.

Caveat: I'd want to see whether that 8% is genuinely low or just early — if a chunk of these buyers are inside their first 30 days, your true mature repeat rate is higher. Pull the repeat rate by monthly cohort before you panic, but the direction is clear: retention first, throttle second.

an0278.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low on Meesho Ads? Same edtech test-prep offer, AOV ₹800, margins ~54%. Six weeks ago CAC was ₹369 and ROAS 2.2, now CAC is ₹700 and ROAS has dropped to 1.1. The CTR just keeps sliding. Is the algorithm throttling me?

The lever isn't bidding or audience — it's fresh creative. New angles, new hooks, not just a recolour of the same ad. A test-prep audience responds to different fears at different moments: score anxiety, time-left-before-exam, parent pressure — give them 3-4 genuinely different angles.

an0280.user: Trying to understand my WhatsApp broadcast / Search push for the gym. Last 30 days I got 670,000 impressions and 11,409 clicks, so CTR is about 1.7%. But out of all that I only got 93 orders, AOV ₹1,850. I'm running broad-match keywords to get reach. Where's it falling apart?
an0280.assistant:
Your CTR of 1.7% is fine — don't touch it. The fall-off is one layer down: 11,409 clicks turned into just 93 orders. That's a 0.82% conversion rate, and that's where the money is leaking.

The cause is sitting in your own setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match buys you reach by matching you to loosely-related searches — people browsing, comparing, half-curious — not people ready to sign up for a gym. So you get a healthy click rate from a crowd that was never going to convert. You're optimising for clicks and getting exactly that: clicks, not members.

The number that proves it is the gap between a normal CTR and a 0.82% conversion. When traffic is high-intent, those two don't diverge this hard. Cheap, abundant clicks at a near-zero conversion rate is the signature of low intent.

The lever is intent, not volume. Tighten to high-intent keywords — "gym near me", "gym membership [your area]", things people type when they're ready to walk in. Add a negative keyword list to choke off the junk searches eating your budget. You'll see impressions and clicks drop, and that's the point — you want fewer, hotter clicks.

One caveat: 93 orders is a small base to redesign everything off. Make the match-type and negatives change first, give it 3-4 weeks, and watch whether conversion rate climbs before you judge it.

an0281.user: Pasting my numbers because I'm losing my mind. Eyewear D2C on Meesho Ads, post-iOS, spent ₹14L last 30 days. Meta's dashboard says my ROAS is 4.4. But Shopify last-click says 1.4. Same period, same spend, completely different story. Which one do I believe? What's wrong?
an0281.assistant:
Nothing's "wrong" — you're refereeing two dashboards that are built to never agree, and trying to pick a winner is the trap.

Meta's 4.4 is generous: it counts modelled conversions and claims credit on a 7-day-click (often plus view-through) window, so it scoops up sales it merely touched. Shopify last-click's 1.4 is the opposite — it hands all the credit to whatever the customer clicked last, usually Google or a direct visit, and gives Meta almost nothing for the demand it actually created up-funnel. Post-iOS, both are guessing more than they admit. The real number sits somewhere between them, and no amount of staring will reconcile them.

So stop trying. The only number that can't lie to you is blended: total spend ÷ actual new customers. Take everything you spent across all channels in the month, divide by the count of genuinely new customers Shopify recorded, and that's your true blended CAC. Manage to that against your contribution per order, and the dashboard civil war stops mattering.

Do this: pull new-customer count from Shopify for the month, divide ₹14L (plus any other ad spend) by it, and anchor every scaling decision on that single figure. Platform ROAS becomes a directional signal, not gospel.

Caveat — blended CAC slightly over-charges paid when you have strong organic/word-of-mouth pulling people in. But it errs on the safe side, which is exactly what you want when two dashboards are lying to you in opposite directions.

an0282.user: Meesho seller here, run Meta ads. Pasting 30 days post-iOS: spend ₹4L, Meta says ROAS 3.6, but my Shopify last-click report says 1.3. The two just don't match and I genuinely can't tell which dashboard is telling me the truth. What's wrong?
an0282.assistant:
Both are telling you a version of the truth, and both are biased — that's why they don't match. You can't fix that by picking a side.

Meta's 3.6 uses modelled conversions on a 7-day-click attribution window, so it claims credit for sales it only assisted. Shopify last-click's 1.3 only credits the final touch before checkout, so it strips Meta of all the demand it created earlier in the journey and hands it to Google or direct. Since iOS broke deterministic tracking, both are estimating. Your real ROAS lives between 1.3 and 3.6 — and no dashboard will ever pin it for you.

The way out is to stop trusting platform ROAS as an absolute and anchor on something neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Total ad spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. Take your ₹4L (plus any other channel spend), divide by the count of brand-new customers Shopify logged this month, and that's the real cost to acquire — no attribution argument required.

Manage to that blended CAC against your contribution per order, and the gap between the two dashboards stops being a crisis and becomes background noise.

One honest caveat: blended CAC charges all your organic and repeat-driven sales against paid spend, so it's slightly pessimistic on paid's true efficiency. That's the safer way to be wrong — better to under-credit your ads than to scale on Meta's flattering 3.6 and find out at month-end the cash didn't show up.

an0286.user: Pet-care D2C on Amazon Ads. My question is simple: how do I lower my CAC? Right now AOV is ₹1,300, gross margin 30%, CAC ₹553, ROAS 2.4, CTR 2.1%. I figure if I can get CAC down the whole thing starts working. What levers should I pull on the ads?

You're aiming at the wrong target. This isn't a CAC problem and no ad lever will save it — the disease is your margin.

Say you crush CAC by 20%, from ₹553 to ₹442 — contribution becomes ₹1,300 × 30% − ₹442 = −₹52. Still underwater. The 30% gross margin is the real story. That's thin for a category carrying physical product, fulfilment and Amazon's cut. A margin problem wearing a marketing costume — you feel it in the ad account because that's where the bleeding shows up, but you cure it upstream.

The lever is the margin itself: cut COGS (renegotiate supplier, better pack sizes, bundle to spread fixed cost), or raise effective price/AOV, or both. Get gross margin from 30% to 40% and your contribution at the same ₹553 CAC flips to ₹1,300 × 40% − ₹553 = −₹33 — close enough that ad optimisation finally matters. At 50% you're at +₹97 and now lowering CAC actually compounds.

Fix the unit economics first. Optimising ads on a 30% margin is rearranging deck chairs.
